blocks.text: JavaScript RegExp Flags
RegExp Modifier Flags

Flags are parameters that can modify how a regex pattern is used,
such as making it case-insensitive or global.
/pattern/flags
JavaScript Regex Flags
Revised July 2025

rows: An upgrade to the /u flag for better Unicode support (new 2025)

blocks.text: Flag Syntax: /pattern/flags

rows: Opening delimiter for the regular expression
Closing delimiter for the regular expression
One or more single modifier flags

blocks.text: RegExp /g Flag (Global)
The /g flag matches all occurrences of the pattern, rather than just the first one.

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: RegExp /i Flag (Insensitive)
The /i flag makes the match case-insensitive: /abc/i matches "abc", "AbC", "ABC".

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: RegExp /d Flag

The /d flag (the Indices flag) is used to find the start and end positions
of substrings captured by regular expression groups.
It does not change the regex match. It provides metadata about the result.

The array returned by exec() or match()
includes an additional indices property: An array of pairs representing the [start, end] index of a specific capture group.

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: You can check if a regex has the /d flag using the hasIndices property.
RegExp /s Flag (Single line/DotAll)

The /s flag allows the . (dot) metacharacter to match newline characters (\n) in addition to any other
character.

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: RegExp /m Flag (Multiline)
The /m (multiline) flag specifies a multiline match.

let text = `Is this

all there

is`

let pattern = /^is/m;
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: The /m flag affects the behavior of ^ and $.
^ specifies a match at the start of a string.
$ specifies a match at the end of a string.

With /m set, ^ and $ will match the start and end of each line,
in a multiline string, in addition to the start and end of the entire string.
RegExp /y Flag (Sticky):
The /y flag performs a "sticky" search from the lastIndex property of the RegExp object.
The /y flag lets a match start at the exact position where the last match ended.

blocks.caption: Examples
Examples

blocks.text: The example above uses a regex metacharacter \w
The meaning of /\w/ is "match an (alphanumeric) word character".
The meaning of /\w+/ is "match one or more word characters".
You will learn more about metacharacters in the next chapters.
RegExp /u Flag (Unicode)
The /u flag enables full Unicode support in a regular expression.

By default, JavaScript RegExp treats 4-byte Unicode characters
(like emojis or less common symbols) as two separate 2-byte "surrogate" code units.

The /u flag treats the pattern as a sequence of Unicode code points,
which is important for correctly handling of characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP).

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: Without the /u flag, regular expressions are not "Unicode-aware".

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: JavaScript 2025 introduced the /v flag as an "upgrade" to the /u flag.
The /v Flag enables more Unicode-related features.
RegExp /v Flag (Unicode Sets)
The /v flag is an upgrade to the /u flag for better Unicode support.
It enables more Unicode-related features.
The new features are:

items: The \p escape sequence matches strings, instead of just characters.

The character class is upgraded to allow intersection, union, and subtraction syntaxes,
as well as matching multiple Unicode characters.

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: Without the /v flag, regular expressions are not "Unicode-aware".

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: RegExp Group Modifiers (?flag)
The (?flag) syntax is a group modifier (inline flag modifier).
It allows for modifying flags in a part of a pattern, rather than to the entire pattern.
(?flags:pattern) enables the flags only for the pattern in the group.

blocks.text: The dotAll Property

The dotAll property returns true
if the /s flag is set.

const pattern = /W3Schools/s;

let result = pattern.dotAll;
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: The global Property

The global property returns true
if the /g flag is set.

const pattern = /W3Schools/g;

let result = pattern.global;
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: The hasIndices Property

The hasIndices property returns true
if the /d flag is set.

const pattern = /W3Schools/d;

let result = pattern.hasIndices;
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: The ignoreCase Property

The ignoreCase property returns true
if the /i flag is set.

const pattern = /W3Schools/i;

let result = pattern.ignoreCase;
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: The multiline Property

The multiline property returns true
if the /m flag is set.

const pattern = /W3Schools/m;

let result = pattern.multiline;
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: The sticky Property

The sticky property returns true
if the /y flag is set.

const pattern = /W3Schools/y;

let result = pattern.sticky;
blocks.caption: Example
